summary: 1955 Forest Service CL-100 series lookout cab on 9,801 ft Eagle Peak in Gila National Forest; replaced a 1929 tower; NHLR-registered 2022; seasonal staffing reported in 2020.

facts.design: USDA Forest Service Standard Plan CL-100 to CL-106 series; 14 by 14 foot steel cab on a 10-foot concrete blockhouse base

access.note: Active Forest Service fire lookout. The sources read do not say whether the cab is open to visitors; check with the Reserve Ranger District before going.

visit.trail_note: Reached by Wilson Canyon Trail #768 and Forest Road 38 (Eagle Peak Road). The Forest Service says the trail and road together are 1.5 miles one way. A road guide calls the road unpaved.

facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service, Gila National Forest (Reserve Ranger District)

events.note: Earlier lookout tower on Eagle Peak, per a Forest Service history cited by Wikipedia and quoted by the westlookouts page
Current CL-100 series cab on a 10-foot base replaced the 1929 tower (NHLR gives 1955 as the build year)
A lookout was stationed on the peak as of April 15, 1967, with a second person to join
Evaluated for the National Register under the Southwest lookouts theme; not eligible due to age
Staffed by seasonal Forest Service employees, per the 2020 New Mexico chapter report
Registered May 22, 2022 as US 1586, NM 44; nominated by Mark Gutzman

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Register calls the base a concrete blockhouse 10 feet high. The westlookouts history calls it a 10-foot cinder block base with a storage room. The story gives the 10-foot height and notes the disagreement.

Wikipedia says NFSR 233 provides access to Eagle Peak Road #38. Dangerous Roads says the 3.2-mile road starts from State Route 233. The Forest Service trail page describes the route without the 233 number, so the story uses the Forest Service description.

notes_for_editor: Staffing rests on a 2020 New Mexico chapter report (seasonal Forest Service employees) and a road guide that says it is staffed every fire season; current 2026 staffing is not confirmed with the Forest Service. No notable fires were found in the sources. The 1929 tower comes from a USFS history quoted by two secondary sites; the Register does not mention it. Access is set to restricted because the sources do not say whether the cab is open to visitors; confirm with the Reserve Ranger District. A Chamber of Commerce directory blurb says it is staffed every fire season; not used. No photo credits recorded (no image URLs read).
